bullets: How a complex number lives on the Argand diagram, and how modulus and argument unlock powers
slides.heading: JC H2 complex numbers: the Argand diagram
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we treat a complex number as a point and an arrow, and by the end you will be able to find a modulus, a principal argument, and the principal argument of a power without falling for the angle wrap-around trap.

bullets: Plot z = x + iy on the Argand diagram and read off its modulus and argument
Use De Moivre: multiplying adds arguments, powers multiply the argument - then wrap into the principal range
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these two things, including the wrap into -180 to 180 degrees.

bullets: Real numbers live on a line - where does 3 + 2i live?
It needs a whole plane: across for the real part, up for the imaginary part
slides.heading: A number that needs a plane
slides.notes: Ask where 3 + 2i could possibly sit if numbers were only a line; take two or three guesses, then say: hold that thought, because the Argand diagram gives every complex number a home.

bullets: z = x + iy: x is the real part, y is the imaginary part, and i^2 = -1
The conjugate of z = x + iy is x - iy: the same point mirrored in the real axis
Modulus |z| is a length and argument arg(z) is an angle - every z has both
slides.heading: One number, two coordinates
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: a complex number packages a length and a direction, and the Argand diagram is where we read both off.

bullets: z = 3 + 2i is the point 3 across the real axis and 2 up the imaginary axis
The journey across then up is the number itself
slides.heading: A complex number is a point on the Argand diagram
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch z travel 3 across the real axis, then 2 up the imaginary axis - the landing point is the number.

bullets: Modulus |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2): Pythagoras on the two legs of the right triangle
slides.heading: Modulus is the distance from the origin
slides.notes: Tell them to watch the green line grow from the origin out to z: that length is the modulus, and the x and iy legs are just a right triangle waiting for Pythagoras.

bullets: Argument arg(z) is the angle the arrow from the origin makes with the positive real axis
The conjugate mirrors the point below the axis, so arg(conjugate of z) = -arg(z)
slides.heading: Argument is the angle; the conjugate mirrors it
slides.notes: Watch the arrow sweep up from the axis to theta, then dive below it: the imaginary part flips sign, and that mirror image is the conjugate.

bullets: Multiplying by i is a quarter turn: 1 goes to i, and again to -1, so i^2 = -1
In general, multiplying multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments; De Moivre turns powers into angle arithmetic
slides.heading: Multiplying rotates and stretches
slides.notes: Follow the radius arrow on the unit circle: each multiplication by i sweeps a quarter turn, and De Moivre is just that pattern written as a rule - multiply the lengths, add the angles.

bullets: Tempting wrong turn: If arg(z) = 100 degrees then arg(z^3) = 300 degrees.
300 degrees is outside the principal range, so wrap it: 300 - 360 = -60 degrees
slides.heading: A common mistake: angles wrap around
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: three hops of 100 degrees do land on the same point as 300 degrees, but the principal Arg must sit in -180 to 180 degrees, so the answer wraps to -60 degrees.

bullets: Step 1: modulus of z = -1 + sqrt(3)i is sqrt(1 + 3) = 2
Step 2: the point is in the second quadrant, so Arg(z) = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees; z = 2(cos 120 degrees + i sin 120 degrees)
slides.heading: Worked example: polar form
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: notice the quadrant check in step 2 - the reference angle is 60 degrees, but the point sits up and to the left, so the principal argument is 120 degrees.

bullets: Find the modulus and principal argument of z = 3 + 4i and of w = -2 + 2i, checking each quadrant first
Careful - a classmate writes If arg(z) = 100 degrees then arg(z^3) = 300 degrees. Explain to them why that is wrong, and give the correct principal value
slides.heading: Your turn: read the diagram, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs two minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: 300 degrees names the right point, so what exactly is wrong with calling it the principal argument?

bullets: Find a modulus and a principal argument from an Argand diagram point, showing the quadrant check
Explain why this claim is wrong: If arg(z) = 100 degrees then arg(z^3) = 300 degrees.
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the words wrap around and -60 degrees in your last answer - if you can explain why the principal Arg must land in -180 to 180 degrees, you have cracked today's lesson.
